opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think the first thing is to be careful about what we mean by "doing research," because it's not one skill. There's generating hypotheses, designing experiments, actually running them, interpreting results, and then the hardest part, deciding what's worth pursuing next. A lot of the excitement around systems like AutoResearch comes from how well they handle the middle of that pipeline. Give them a well-defined setup, say a training script and a metric to improve, and they can iterate tirelessly: tweak hyperparameters, try architectural variants, read the logs, try again. That's genuinely useful, and in some narrow settings they'll find improvements a human might have missed simply because they can run so many more trials.

But I'd separate that from research taste. When I assess these systems, I look at a few things. First, is the improvement real, or is the model overfitting to the evaluation? If you let an agent optimize a single number long enough, it gets very good at gaming that number, so you need held-out evaluations and some skepticism. Second, can it explain why something worked in a way that transfers? A result that holds at one scale and disappears at the next isn't much of a finding. Third, and this is the one I care about most, does it ever change the question? The most important research moments usually come from noticing that you were optimizing the wrong thing, or that an anomaly in the data points somewhere new. Today's agents are much better at hill-climbing within a framing than at stepping outside it.

So my rough assessment is that they're already strong research assistants, almost like a very fast, very diligent junior researcher who never gets tired of running ablations. They're not yet independent researchers. The way I'd measure progress is less "did the loss go down" and more "did it produce an insight that a senior researcher would find surprising and that holds up when someone else tries to reproduce it." When we start seeing that consistently, that's when the conversation really changes.

r001.rationale: The response says AutoResearch systems are better at optimizing within a given framing than at changing the question, but it does not clearly characterize their generated research ideas as lacking creativity.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that it depends a lot on what you mean by "research," and that word is doing a lot of work right now.

If you mean the part of research that is search over a well-defined space, then systems like AutoResearch are already genuinely useful. Give them a codebase, a benchmark, and a metric, and they'll propose a change, run it, look at the number, and iterate. They don't get tired, they don't get attached to their hypotheses, and they'll try the thing a grad student would be too embarrassed to try. In that setting you can get a surprising amount of real progress overnight. I've seen cases where the loop found a tweak that a competent human team had been circling for weeks.

But that's the inner loop. The thing I'd push back on is calling that the whole of research. The hard parts, in my experience, are upstream and downstream of that loop. Upstream is choosing the question: deciding that this metric is the one worth moving, that this benchmark isn't already saturated or gamed, that the direction connects to something that matters in a year. Downstream is interpretation: noticing that the improvement is real but the reason you thought it would work is wrong, and that the wrongness is actually the interesting finding. Models today are still weak at both ends. They'll optimize the objective you handed them with great enthusiasm, including when the objective is subtly broken.

There's also a taste problem. When a human researcher gets a result that looks too good, they get suspicious. When an automated loop gets a result that looks too good, it often gets more confident. So you end up needing a human whose main job is skepticism, which is a bit of a role reversal. The model does the experiments and the person does the doubting.

So my assessment is something like: as a research assistant that owns the experimental loop, these systems are already better than most people expect, and they're going to get a lot better quickly because that loop is easy to measure. As an autonomous scientist that picks the problem, knows when it's fooling itself, and changes direction when the world changes, we're not there, and I'd be cautious about anyone who claims we are based on a few benchmark wins.

The place I find most interesting is the middle. Can you get the model to propose which questions to ask, and then have a human choose among them? That division of labor seems to work well right now, and it's where I'd expect the real productivity gains to show up over the next couple of years.

r001.rationale: The response says models are weak at choosing research questions and interpreting results, but it does not characterize their generated research ideas as lacking creativity.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between running experiments and deciding what research is worth doing. If you give a model a clear objective, a way to measure progress, and an environment where it can modify code and run experiments, it can do a useful part of the research loop. It can try an idea, look at the result, and use that feedback to decide what to try next.

But that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it can identify an important problem or recognize when the metric you’ve chosen is missing something. A system might improve a benchmark without producing a result that generalizes. So I’d want to see whether its findings hold up across different settings, whether it compares against strong baselines, and whether the improvement survives independent replication.

The exciting possibility is that these systems make it much cheaper to test ideas. That could let researchers explore directions they otherwise wouldn’t have time for. But I’d judge their research ability by the quality of the discoveries they produce, rather than simply by how many experiments they can run autonomously.

r001.rationale: The response questions whether models can identify important problems and emphasizes validating discoveries, but it does not characterize their generated research ideas as lacking creativity.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d separate running experiments from deciding which experiments are worth running. If you give a system a clear objective, a codebase, and a way to measure progress, it can propose changes, run experiments, inspect the results, and iterate. That’s a meaningful part of research, and models are getting better at it.

The harder question is whether they can identify an important problem, question the assumptions behind a benchmark, or recognize that an unexpected result points to something more interesting than the original goal. Improving a score doesn’t necessarily mean you’ve produced new understanding.

So I’d assess these systems by whether their results hold up under independent testing, whether the findings generalize, and how much human guidance they need. I’m excited about their ability to shorten the experimental cycle. But I’d distinguish that from demonstrating the full range of judgment that research requires.

r001.rationale: The response says models struggle to identify important problems and exercise research judgment, but it does not clearly characterize the research ideas they generate as lacking creativity.
